cards.q: What are OSPF LSAs and why are the types important?
cards.a: LSAs (Link State Advertisements) are the building blocks of the OSPF LSDB. Each type describes a different part of the topology or reachability. Knowing who originates which type and where it lives (intra-area, backbone, external) is core ENCOR material, especially Types 1-7.

cards.q: Who originates each of OSPF LSA Types 1 through 7?
cards.a: Type 1 Router LSA is by every router; Type 2 Network LSA by the DR; Type 3 Summary LSA by the ABR; Type 4 ASBR-Summary LSA by the ABR; Type 5 AS-external LSA by the ASBR; Type 6 Group-membership (MOSPF, obsolete); Type 7 NSSA-external LSA by the ASBR in an NSSA.

cards.q: Where is each OSPF LSA type flooded?
cards.a: Type 1 and 2 are flooded within the area only. Type 3 and 4 are generated by the ABR and flooded between areas. Type 5 is flooded across the whole OSPF domain except stub areas. Type 7 is flooded within the NSSA only and converted to Type 5 by the ABR at the exit.

cards.q: Map each OSPF LSA type to its show ip route code.
cards.a: Type 1/2 produce O (intra-area); Type 3 produces O IA (inter-area); Type 5 produces O E1 or O E2 (external); Type 7 produces O N1 or O N2 (NSSA external).

cards.q: What is the difference between OSPF E1 and E2 external routes?
cards.a: E2 is the default and uses only the external cost advertised in the LSA. E1 includes the path cost to the ASBR, so the total cost differs depending on where you are in the network. The same E1/E2 distinction applies to N1/N2 for NSSA routes.

cards.q: What is Type 4 LSA used for?
cards.a: The Type 4 ASBR-Summary LSA tells routers how to reach an ASBR. It is needed only when an external route's forwarding address is not directly reachable, so the cost to external routes can be computed.

Type 9 is link-local scope (e.g., LDP/segment routing), Type 10 is area-local scope (TE/MPLS Traffic Engineering), and Type 11 is domain scope. On the exam they are identified as being used for MPLS-TE/extensions, not routing basics.

cards.q: What show command displays each OSPF LSA type?
cards.a: show ip ospf database for all; router for Type 1, network for Type 2, summary for Type 3, asbr-summary for Type 4, external for Type 5, nssa-external for Type 7, and link-state for ages/sequence per LSA.

cards.q: Which OSPF LSA types are blocked in stub, totally stubby, and NSSA areas?
cards.a: Stub and totally stubby areas block Type 5 (and Type 4), with totally stubby also blocking Type 3. NSSA areas block inbound Type 5 but allow Type 7. That area filtering is the whole point of these area types.

cards.q: Who originates the Type 2 Network LSA?
cards.a: The DR originates Type 2, describing the broadcast/NBMA segment and the routers attached to it. It is not originated by every router.

cards.q: Why is the Type 4 LSA needed?
cards.a: The Type 4 ASBR-Summary LSA is needed to tell routers how to reach the ASBR, so they can compute the cost to external routes whose forwarding address is not directly reachable.

cards.q: Where does the Type 7 to Type 5 translation happen in an NSSA?
cards.a: The translation from Type 7 to Type 5 happens at the ABR, not the ASBR. The ASBR inside the NSSA originates Type 7, and the ABR converts it to Type 5 when flooding outside the area.

cards.q: What route code does each LSA type produce and is E2 or E1 the default?
cards.a: O from Type 1/2, O IA from Type 3, O E1/O E2 from Type 5, O N1/O N2 from Type 7. E2 (external cost only) is the default; E1 includes the cost to the ASBR.
